reason: The text depicts Yahweh as a concrete, particularistic, and highly engaged deity rather than a universal, omniscient, abstract one. Yahweh manifests as a pillar of cloud and fire (עַמּוּד הֶעָנָן וְהַחֹשֶׁךְ, עַמּוּד אֵשׁ)—physically present and visible. The deity performs specific, temporal military actions: moving the pillar, looking down on the Egyptian camp (וַיַּשְׁקֵף), stirring up (וַיְנַעֵר) and destroying the Egyptians through the sea. These are concrete, anthropomorphic actions located in a particular historical moment. Furthermore, Yahweh acts exclusively on behalf of Israel against Egypt, which demonstrates particularism rather than universalism. There is no evidence of omniscience; instead, the text shows deliberate observation and sequential action at specific moments.
